If you look at this small harbor scene, you are looking at the painting that accidentally named a movement. In 1874 a group of painters, tired of being judged by the official Salon, organized an independent exhibition in Paris, in the former studio of a well-known photographer. This canvas was hanging there, with a simple title that mentioned an impression of a sunrise. One critic seized on that word. Writing a mocking review, he suggested that an impression was all the painter had managed, since a finished painting was clearly beyond him, and he called the whole group Impressionists. The insult stuck, and within a few years the painters were using it themselves. Now, before we move on, I want you to do something. Walk right up to the canvas, as close as the line on the floor allows, and look at the water. You will see separate, loose strokes that do not describe anything. Then step back five or six paces, slowly. Watch the strokes turn back into a harbor, a few boats and a rising orange sun.

Last week we saw the Impressionists. Today, the long road that followed, and I want to start with a warning. The story of modern art is usually told far too neatly, as a straight line of heroes, each artist handing a torch to the next until we arrive at abstraction. It did not happen like that. Many paths were tried and abandoned, and several of the people who tried them have only recently returned to the textbooks. What later painters really took from the Impressionists was a kind of freedom: the visible brushstroke, and the right to paint ordinary modern life. What they rejected, quite quickly, was the idea that a painting should record a passing moment of light. They wanted something more solid, or more personal, or more structured. And underneath all of it runs what I like to call the quiet revolution, which is flatness. Gradually, painters stopped pretending that the canvas was a window onto a deep space, and they accepted it for what it had always been: a flat surface covered with paint.
